new.n: Berrien County fair ground, Niles (1858 to the 1860s)
new.pl: R. C. Paine's land west of the cemetery, where Tenth St extended south meets it at the SE corner of the 1859 city plat
new.v: Fairground coin and token drops from 19th-century county fairs
new.st: In 1858 the Berrien County Agricultural Society bought R. C. Paine's land 'west of the cemetery' for its fair ground. Its 1858 statement lists fencing and 'grubbing, ditching, excavating lake, draining, filling in, grading track', so the grounds had a dug pond with a graded track. In December 1860 a petition asked to open 'Tenth St. to the fair ground'. On the 1859 City of Niles inset, Tenth Street extended south reaches the ground west of the cemetery; the 1945 USGS sheet shows open ground there.
new.t: The dug pond and track bed could still show on 1938 air photos or lidar. Today's use not yet checked: look-only if built over. Gathering grounds: under the oldest trees, the flat where the crowd stood, the track edges and where wagons parked.
src: History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties (1880)

new.pl: Jennings (ghost village), GNIS point; spot not placed
new.st: Wood-cutter turned hermit John Larson was said to have turned a Swedish inheritance into American gold and buried $10,000 to $75,000 near Jennings; 'no trace has been since found'. When Jennings was trucked away to Cadillac about 1923 a quiet hunt went on, and his son, seeing the move in a newsreel, came back and dug for days, with conflicting rumours of success. Pin is approximate (village point), not the spot itself.
new.t: One printed account, undated; the Cadillac Evening News of 1923 is being checked. Old Jennings Cemetery (south of the village) is graves: look-only.
src: Undated clipping c.1923, paper unnamed (TreasureNet thread 626432)

set.st: Four men robbed the Wabeno State Bank of $32,000 in cash and negotiable securities on 15 July 1921 (first put at $27,000). The gang was Willis and Lawrence Lesperance of Oconto and Chalmers and "Frenchie" Yaeger of Green Bay. Willis Lesperance and one Yaeger were taken on 23 July and lodged at Crandon; Lawrence Lesperance and Chalmers Yaeger were caught at Chippewa Falls in August. Sentences of 25 years each at Crandon were reported in 1921; a jail-break attempt at Crandon followed in September 1921, and in 1922 Lawrence drew a year at Waupun as an accessory. By their confession they buried the loot in the woods some distance from Wabeno while posses were on their trail. In July 1922 Lawrence was brought from Waupun for a day-long search that found nothing. In August 1922 berry pickers found a weather-beaten touring car on an abandoned logging trail in the wilderness about 20 miles east of Wabeno, several miles west of Athelstane, and the search moved there. Pin is approximate (town or township only), not the spot itself.

src: Northern Wisconsin Advertiser (Wabeno), 26 Aug 1921 p. 2; 23 Sep 1921 p. 2; 8 Sep 1922 p. 2

His father, 48 years on the homestead from about 1864, had died about 1912 apparently without money even for his burial. The 1916 Dakota atlas shows no Rechenberg on the Mendota plate, so the farm is still unplaced.

cr-homer-bandit-cave.t: The 1901 telling puts the cave about 1.5 miles from Homer, so look along the bluffs 2-2.5 km from the village as well as close behind it.

tw-strolfer-superior-1897.st: He died on a Monday night in December 1897 in a dilapidated shanty four miles east of Superior. A former Chicago tailor, he came to Superior about 1871, took a government quarter section (title about 1882), traded 120 acres for Superior town lots that sold in the boom for about $100,000, and kept 40 acres, where the shanty stood. Weeks of searching found nothing.
tw-strolfer-superior-1897.t: No GLO patent exists under Strolfer or Stroelfer (BLM), so the land came by private deed; a Douglas County deed index or an 1890s Superior directory would place the 40.
src: "Looking for a Miser's Hoard," Chicago Tribune, 24 Dec 1897, p. 8 (Newspapers.com 349834757) (Superior, Dec 21)
